findings.passage: In 2015, after a Playboy interview was reported as a boast, Hartnett told USA Today, [as quoted by ComicBook.com](https://comicbook.com/comicbook/news/josh-hartnett-clarifies-comments-on-turning-down-christopher-nol), that he did not regret Superman.
findings.problem: The evidence record lists unopened sources as support. C80 cites S32 (Playboy 2015) and C48 cites S36 (USA Today 2015); both are marked access: unavailable, and no stage opened them. The article handles this correctly ("as quoted by ComicBook.com"), and the wording checks out against S23. But the release gate requires every source a claim cites to be opened and context-checked, and I cannot honestly report S32 or S36 as opened. As it stands, the record says these claims rest on originals nobody read.
findings.acceptance_test: In evidence-edit.json, C80 and C48 cite only opened sources (S23, plus any original actually opened and checked). S32 and S36 may stay in the source list as unavailable, but no claim's source_ids includes them. No change to the article is needed.

findings.passage: Cooke met him in April 2002, near the end of the publicity run.
findings.problem: S03 was published on April 21, 2002 and does not give the meeting date. The meeting was at a New York press junket for 40 Days and 40 Nights while the film was already on cinema displays, so it probably came before April. "Met him in April 2002" adds a precision the source does not have.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence dates the piece, not the meeting (for example, "In a profile published in April 2002, Cooke described him..."), or cites a source for the meeting date. C13 is updated to match.

findings.passage: His only explanation then was a shrug: "Well, we're all on a journey."
findings.problem: Cooke never describes a shrug. She writes only that he "clearly dislikes talking about the film". Even as a figure of speech, "a shrug" adds a gesture to a sourced scene.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence gives his answer without an unrecorded gesture (for example, "His only explanation then: 'Well, we're all on a journey.'"), or uses Cooke's own words about his reluctance to discuss the film. C140 is updated to match.

findings.passage: He calls talking about his own career "self-indulgent," and on _Below_ he asked that his character not be "constantly talking about his trauma."
findings.problem: The Below request was about a fictional fisherman. He grounded it in regional realism: "a reticence amongst people that live kind of off the beaten path outside of big cities to complain about their own situation" (CBC Q, October 2026; confirmed by my own transcription). Set beside the "self-indulgent" line as evidence against Type 4, it implies a statement about his own self-focus that he did not make. The evidence record's alternative for C41 already notes this.
findings.acceptance_test: Either the Below clause carries his stated reason (Minnesota-style reticence he wanted the character to have) and is framed as a taste, not as self-description, or the Type 4 rebuttal drops it and rests on the "self-indulgent" line and the community evidence.

findings.passage: Not taking part is how a Nine resists; a hard fight is not, so the studio record is not scored here.
findings.problem: At about 4,030 words the body runs well past the standard's 2,000-3,500 target. The editing that made it honest also made it heavier: stacked attribution clauses and audit-voice lines ("is not scored here", "This profile reads them as one worry", "so treat the detail as reported") slow "Saying no to the capes" and "Why not Type 9?". That is the main reason the writing score is 7.5, which helps hold the overall score below the release floor.
findings.acceptance_test: The body is at or under about 3,600 words with every protected passage, every inventoried quotation and every secondhand label kept. Audit-voice phrases are rewritten as reader-facing sentences, so no paragraph has more than two hedging or provenance clauses unless a quote requires them. The shifting-reasons list in "Saying no to the capes" reads as a progression, not a ledger.

enneagram.passage: Run that test on the 2002 retreat and it comes out close to even. His words for it are a Nine's: it "had more to do with just plain sanity," he told Stiles, and "it didn't feel entirely healthy. So I just sort of took a step back," he told Hollywood Authentic. What he left, and where he went, read more like a Six's: intrusion he "didn't know how to protect myself" from, and a return home because "I wanted to be myself amongst people that I knew." A Nine retreats to be left in peace. A Six retreats toward people he can count on.
